Otolaryngology · published research

Septoplasty

A 62-person controlled study reported less pain at six to 24 hours after perioperative laser treatment. A rat study found fewer p53-positive hippocampal neurons after surgery and early treatment, which is not evidence of improved human septal healing.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 62-person controlled study reported less pain at six to 24 hours after perioperative laser treatment. A rat study found fewer p53-positive hippocampal neurons after surgery and early treatment, which is not evidence of improved human septal healing.

Summary of the Evidence

Two mapped publications address septoplasty: one human controlled study and one rat experiment. They evaluate different outcomes, so the animal stress-marker result does not replicate the human pain finding. There is no standalone cell study.

Human and clinical evidence

Kastyro et al. studied 62 patients, 31 per group, after septoplasty. The PBM group received treatment at three early postoperative time points and again intranasally at 48 hours. The authors reported lower pain at six to 24 hours and changes in heart-rate variability compared with the control group (2021). The report is a controlled clinical study, but its design does not provide strong evidence for durable recovery or complications. It does not establish that pain reduction improves nasal function or healing.

Animal evidence

Kotov et al. studied rats after septoplasty and reported fewer p53-positive hippocampal neurons on day six in animals receiving early PBM than in surgery-only controls (2025). This is a stress-related brain-tissue marker, not a direct measure of septal healing or patient recovery.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified among the mapped records.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human protocol used pulsed 890-nm laser treatment over the nose at 3, 6, and 24 hours, followed by intranasal 630-nm red light at 48 hours. The rat study addresses a distinct biological endpoint. These different wavelengths, routes, and endpoints do not define one standardized postoperative protocol.

Interpretation

The small human study suggests possible early pain reduction, but evidence for clinically important recovery is very low. The animal study does not confirm the clinical outcome.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reducing postoperative pain Very low for effects on recovery or long-term outcomes
Publications and records2 mapped publications.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One controlled study of 62 patients reported lower pain after postoperative nasal PBM, while one rat study measured a hippocampal stress marker rather than septal healing. The human report is small and allocation details do not establish a robust blinded randomized comparison. Replication should use sham treatment and functional recovery outcomes.

  • Animal1 (rat) study of hippocampal p53-positive neurons after surgery.
  • No standalone in-vitro study.
